newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Jews commemorate victims of Holocaust.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Jews commemorate victims of Holocaust.

text.p: Members of Bulgaria's small Jewish community gathered at Sofia's synagogue on Monday to commemorate the victims of the Nazi Holocaust and to remember those who helped save them from the death camps.
Public pressure saved Bulgaria's Jews from deportation during World War Two, although the Balkan state was allied with Germany.
"This is an extraordinary day for me -- a day of pain and excitement, I feel proud of my Jewish origin and sad for the Jews' tragic destiny," said Sofia Koen, 17, who led the service.
More than 500 Jews attended the service at the city centre synagogue, which was restored and reopened last year. Six Jewish children lit six candles to commemorate the six million Holocaust victims.
Edi Shvartz, head of the Shalom Group of Bulgarian Jews said the figures were not just statistics as each of them represented "a life, and dreams for the future which were killed".
"The pain in the hearts of Jewish people is still alive and we all pray for such a tragedy not be repeated again," said one elderly man at the service, Moris Natan.
Bulgaria's wartime government refused to hand over its 50,000 Jewish citizens to the Nazis in 1943 despite its military alliance with Germany.
"We shall never forget that Bulgaria saved its Jews and did not allow their deportation," said David Levi.
Yaakov Djerassi, president of the Zion Jewish organisation, said the role of Bulgaria and its wartime King Boris III had not received the recognition it deserved.
"Bulgaria's people and the Bulgarian King did a heroic deed in saving their Jews and after so many years I think it is high time that the whole world should recognise this," he said.
Bulgarian Jews had to wear Star of David badges, many businesses and professions were forbidden them and men were drafted to build roads, but none died in the Nazi death camps.
After World War Two, Bulgaria's Jews emigrated to Israel, and now the community numbers no more than 7,000.

Most Bulgarian Jews are Sephardic, descendents of the Jews forced out of Spain in 1492. They were invited by the Ottomans, who offered religious freedom in exchange for the practice of their skills as artisans and merchants.
